titulo.texto: Hemicycle to Juárez: Carrara Marble for the Centennial

frase_gancho.texto: Twelve marble columns form a semicircle dedicated to Benito Juárez, inaugurated during the Centennial celebrations of Independence.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue toward the western side of the park, heading for Balderas Street. At the corner with Colón stands the museum that holds a mural about this very Alameda.

como_llegar.texto: Continue toward the southern edge of the park, the one facing Juárez Avenue. A marble monument with columns awaits you there.

guion_corto.texto: The dedication engraved at the center of this monument reads: Al Benemérito Benito Juárez, la Patria. It is a Carrara marble ensemble on the southern edge of the Alameda. It was inaugurated on September eighteenth, nineteen ten, during the celebrations of the Centennial of Independence. It consists of twelve Doric columns arranged in a semicircle and, at the center, Juárez seated and crowned with laurel by allegorical figures. Lower down there is an eagle and two lions on a base with step-fret patterns inspired by pre-Hispanic art. It took the place of a Moorish kiosk that had been dismantled as early as November nineteen oh nine. Porfirio Díaz, who had had political differences with Juárez, promoted this tribute.

guion_largo.texto:
Look at the medallion at the center. There is the dedication: Al Benemérito Benito Juárez, la Patria. Benemérito means worthy of being remembered. It is the title by which Juárez is remembered, the liberal president who led the defense of the Republic against the Second Empire. That empire, the one of Maximilian of Habsburg, ended with his execution by firing squad in eighteen sixty-seven.

Juárez died in the National Palace on July eighteenth, eighteen seventy-two. His remains were buried on the twenty-third of that month in the San Fernando Cemetery. That is why this hemicycle is a tribute and not a tomb.

The monument was inaugurated on September eighteenth, nineteen ten. It was part of the Centennial of Independence celebrations organized by President Porfirio Díaz. Construction began in nineteen oh six. That year the avenue took its current name, Avenida Juárez.

The project was commissioned to the architect Guillermo Heredia. The sculptures are by the Italian Alessandro Lazzerini. More than one thousand six hundred blocks of Carrara marble were used, from Italy, a region famous for centuries for its white marble. That whiteness is what gives it the look of an ancient temple in the middle of the park.

The structure is neoclassical, with a strong Greek influence. A hemicycle is simply a half-circle-shaped space, and here that semicircle embraces the central figure. Twelve Doric columns support an entablature. The Doric order is the simplest of Greek architecture, and its sobriety gives the ensemble a solemn air. At the center, Juárez appears seated and is crowned by allegorical figures. Lower down there is an eagle with outstretched wings on a base with step-fret patterns inspired by pre-Hispanic art, and on either side, two lions.

Before this ensemble was built, the Moorish Kiosk stood on this spot. It was dismantled as early as November nineteen oh nine and today it is in the Santa María la Ribera neighborhood. The kiosk had been installed in the Alameda in nineteen oh five.

There is a curious fact. For decades the monument was the setting for the National Lottery drawings. When the lottery moved to its own building, the Hemicycle became, above all, a backdrop for photographs.

There is also a political story. Porfirio Díaz had had differences with Juárez, and even so he promoted this tribute at the Centennial. It has been read as an attempt to give Juárez a central place in the nation's history. Whatever the intention, today it is a favorite backdrop for photographs in the Alameda.

At the Diego Rivera Mural Museum, the next stop, you will find Juárez among the figures of a mural about this very Alameda. Maximilian of Habsburg and Porfirio Díaz also appear there. The Alameda, with its Hemicycle and its fountains, once again becomes a place where the memory of Mexico gathers.

texto.Key fact: twelve columns in a semicircle, on the southern edge of the Alameda

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Hemicycle to Juárez is the tomb of President Benito Juárez.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Juárez died on July 18, 1872 and was buried in the San Fernando Cemetery; the Hemicycle is a tribute monument inaugurated in 1910.
